records.doc: Formal statements and proofs, in Lean 4 with Mathlib, about the normalizers in SL₂(ℝ) of the groups Γ_Δ(N) between Γ₁(N) and Γ₀(N), and the quotients Nor(Γ_Δ(N))/Γ_Δ(N), which for −1 ∈ Δ are the modular automorphism groups of the curves X_Δ(N): the matrices allowed by the generalized Newman bound h_Δ form a group M_Δ = D⁻¹Γ₀(n_Δ)⁺D, D = diag(h_Δ, 1), which contains Nor(Γ_Δ(N)) and contains Γ₀(N) with finite index, so Nor(Γ_Δ(N))/Γ_Δ(N) is finite for every Δ; its order is [(ℤ/N)ˣ : Δ] times the number of pairs (σ, H), with σ in a fixed set of representatives of Γ₀(N)\SL₂(ℤ) and H a Hermite normal form, such that σH normalizes Γ_Δ(N); and h_Δ = h(N) except under three explicit conditions on N and Δ. 11 theorems, no sorry, only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

records.name: PalomarResults.LossyShell.endpoint_trace_equivalence
records.entry_name: Lossy Distance-Shell Tomography on Paths: Recovery from Mean and Covariance
records.doc: A substantive Lean development of two-leg identifiability under independent relay deletion and nearest-surviving-ancestor bypass. An interior path sensor observes anonymous counts at each contracted hop, superimposing both legs. For every known real survival probability strictly between zero and one, the mean and covariance identify the unordered pair of natural-valued leg populations. A sparse interface needs only the covariance diagonal and one adaptively selected column. The concrete law is a finite sum over independent Bernoulli relay masks. Ten selected statements additionally establish mean/fold equivalence, endpoint trace and degenerate-probability semantics, actual-model variance bounds, conditional integer reconstruction recurrences, and a logarithmic randomized-testing lower bound for actual paths of every length at least two. The full finite-sample probability guarantee is not claimed.

records.name: theorem1
records.entry_name: GromovMilman
records.doc: Formalization of Theorem 1 (the Gromov–Milman conjecture on polynomials restricted to subspaces) from Dol'nikov–Karasev, "Dvoretzky type theorems for multivariate polynomials and sections of convex bodies" (arXiv:1009.0392): for any even d > 0 and any k, there exists n(d, k) such that every homogeneous polynomial of degree d on R^n (n >= n(d, k)) restricts on some k-dimensional subspace V to a scalar multiple of (x_1^2 + ... + x_n^2)^(d/2). The formalization provides an unconditional, constructive proof without sorry or external topological black boxes: Carlsson's theorem on non-abelian 2-groups is eliminated in favor of an elementary abelian Dold-type Borsuk–Ulam theorem ((Z/2)^r) proved from scratch on chain complexes and applied inductively level-by-level to iterated wreath products via block-structured join embeddings.

records.name: Collectionwise.exists_open_expansion
records.entry_name: Paracompact expansion and collectionwise separation
records.doc: Every locally finite indexed family of arbitrary subsets of a paracompact topological space admits a locally finite open expansion with the same index type, without separation assumptions. In a paracompact normal space, a discrete closed family admits a discrete locally finite open expansion whose closures are pairwise disjoint and lie in prescribed open neighborhoods. Consequently every paracompact Hausdorff space is collectionwise normal. Index and ambient types may be empty and have independent universes; the family has unrestricted cardinality. These are classical results; no novelty is claimed.

records.name: SystolicGrowth.systolic_growth_lower_bound
records.entry_name: Systolic growth in every genus
records.doc: This repository introduces and formally proves the lower bound 4/3 for the limit inferior of the supremal hyperbolic systole in genus g divided by log g. At present, this formalization is the theorem's only public statement and proof. This metadata records the result as an original proof; the published papers below are cited only as background for ingredients. The proof combines arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces, uniform representations by comparable prime cubes, and surface gluing followed by a smooth conformal change to curvature minus one that preserves the systole lower bound.

records.name: ListEdgeColouring.gale_shapley
records.entry_name: Galvin's theorem, the Dinitz problem and stable matchings
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of Galvin's theorem that the list chromatic index of a finite bipartite graph equals its maximum degree (if every edge has a list of at least Δ colours, a proper edge colouring can be chosen from the lists), of its corollary solving the Dinitz problem (an n × n array with lists of n symbols per cell admits a choice with distinct symbols in every row and column), and of the Gale–Shapley theorem on the existence of stable matchings with strict preferences and incomplete acceptability lists, which provides the kernels in Galvin's argument. Mathlib has line graphs and colourings but none of these results.

records.name: PersistentSOS.radius_eq_norm
records.entry_name: Persistent failure of Euclidean quartic SOS exactness
records.doc: An explicit rational homogeneous cubic with 25 monomials in 14 real variables has maximum one on the Euclidean unit sphere and admits a positive degree-four moment functional with value 500753357629/500000000000. For every positive real regularization parameter, quadratic strength and cubic strength, the associated quartic has an explicitly attained global minimum whose shift is not a sum of squares of real polynomials. A quantitative strict separation bounds every SOS lower bound. The polynomial is stationary at zero with negative definite Hessian. A second explicit 25-term cubic, certified by the same rational functional, gives a unique global minimizer with positive-definite Hessian there and persistent SOS failure for all positive parameters. The exact sphere maximizers are classified. The proof combines an elementary quadratic-map contraction, a rational moment certificate, an ordinary SOS degree bound and an all-parameter radial factorization.

records.name: SolidGridHam.HP.decideHamPath_correct
records.entry_name: Hamiltonian s–t paths in solid grid graphs are decidable in polynomial time
records.doc: A computable algorithm, decideHamPath, that decides whether a solid grid graph (a finite set of lattice points with no holes, with an edge between points at distance 1) has a Hamiltonian path between two given distinct points, with a Lean 4 proof that it is correct. The problem was posed by Itai, Papadimitriou and Szwarcfiter (1982). The algorithm extends Sheffield's height-function algorithm for Hamiltonian cycles: each endpoint gets a phantom edge to a missing neighbour, and an endpoint with all eight neighbours present becomes a hole whose defect (a vortex) is handled by a slit height and a search over flip classes. The registered statement is correctness. The library also proves a polynomial step bound, 5 220 000 (|V| + 3)^6, for cost functions written beside the algorithm, and formalizes the Umans–Lenhart algorithm for Hamiltonian cycles in solid grid graphs.

records.name: LinearStochastic.Palomar.classification
records.entry_name: A Unified Kalman-Type Classification of Controllability for Linear Stochastic Systems
records.doc: Formalization of a finite algebraic classification of approximate, approximate null, exact null, and exact controllability for finite-dimensional linear stochastic systems with constant coefficients and independent Brownian drivers. A decreasing subspace sequence gives a common obstruction for the first three properties; exact controllability additionally requires full row rank of the stacked diffusion-control matrix. The development also covers stochastic integration, forward and backward equations, duality, finite rank tests, null feedback, and polynomial small-time energy bounds. The independent Palomar statement and its solution compile with Lean v4.35.0-rc2 and canonical Mathlib. Complete sandboxed mechanical preflight and editorial review are separate requirements; no registration is claimed.

records.name: DividingCompartments.Paper.main_quantitative
records.entry_name: Survival and transience above the compartment-division threshold
records.doc: Survival and transience are established throughout the strictly supercritical regime of the noncoagulating compartment model of Anderson, Howells and Rojas La Luz (https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10223v4, Remark 4.8). Compartments produce molecules at rate b, degrade them at rate d per molecule, exit at rate e, and divide at rate f per molecule, with arbitrary conservative allocation between the daughters. For b,e,f > 0 and d >= 0 with bf > e(e+d), every finite nonempty family has positive probability of eternal survival, with an explicit product lower bound. For positive immigration intensity and any distribution of finite immigrant contents, the process is nonexplosive and the expected total physical occupation time of every compartment-count state has an explicit finite bound. This establishes the transience conjectured in Remark 4.8 without a moment assumption on immigrant contents. The quantitative bounds use a positive eigenweight of the mean system and a bounded multiplicative barrier; a distribution-dependent immigration constant sharpens the uniform occupation bound.

records.entry_name: Survival and transience above the compartment-division threshold
records.doc: Survival and transience are established throughout the strictly supercritical regime of the noncoagulating compartment model of Anderson, Howells and Rojas La Luz (https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10223v4, Remark 4.8). Compartments produce molecules at rate b, degrade them at rate d per molecule, exit at rate e, and divide at rate f per molecule, with arbitrary conservative allocation between the daughters. For b,e,f > 0 and d >= 0 with bf > e(e+d), every finite nonempty family has positive probability of eternal survival, with an explicit product lower bound. For positive immigration intensity and any distribution of finite immigrant contents, the process is nonexplosive and the expected total physical occupation time of every compartment-count state has an explicit finite bound. This establishes the transience conjectured in Remark 4.8 without a moment assumption on immigrant contents. The quantitative bounds use a positive eigenweight of the mean system and a bounded multiplicative barrier; a distribution-dependent immigration constant sharpens the uniform occupation bound.

Compartments produce molecules at rate b, degrade them at rate d per molecule, exit at rate e, and divide at rate f per molecule, with arbitrary conservative allocation between the daughters. For b,e,f > 0 and d >= 0 with bf > e(e+d), every finite nonempty family has positive probability of eternal survival, with an explicit product lower bound. For positive immigration intensity and any distribution of finite immigrant contents, the process is nonexplosive and the expected total physical occupation time of every compartment-count state has an explicit finite bound. This establishes the transience conjectured in Remark 4.8 without a moment assumption on immigrant contents. The quantitative bounds use a positive eigenweight of the mean system and a bounded multiplicative barrier; a distribution-dependent immigration constant sharpens the uniform occupation bound.

records.name: SigmaCompact.exists_compact_trap
records.entry_name: Omega-bounded Sigma-products and a sharp compactness criterion
records.doc: For arbitrary T1 omega-bounded factors with an explicit product basepoint, the countable-support Sigma-product is omega-bounded and countably compact. Every countable family is trapped, together with its ambient closure, in a closed compact coordinate box using one countable support. For compact Hausdorff factors, the Sigma-product is compact if and only if only countably many factors contain a point different from the basepoint. Uncountable discrete Boolean Sigma-products are countably compact but not compact. The index and factor universes are independent; the empty index and empty countable subsets are allowed. No first-countability or separability premise is added.

records.name: TWSPeriodic.convolution_opNorm
records.entry_name: Exact db2 cascade norms and an optimal uniform constant
records.doc: Exact supremum-operator norms for the undecimated periodic db2 cascade. For every level j and every period N at least the support, the norm is c_j^d, where c_j = 1651/1395 - (4/63)4^{-j} + (1/180)16^{-j} - (1/1736)32^{-j}. For every positive period, aliasing included, the norm is at most (1651/1395)^d, and that power is the least constant with this uniform role. The free mass is strictly increasing, converges to 1651/1395, and the gap is at most (4/63)4^{-j}. Dimension zero is exactly 1. N at least the support is sufficient, not claimed necessary, and one fixed period is not claimed to attain the limit. At dimension zero the least-constant conclusion is 1 ≤ B; it does not force B = 1. The level-one kernel is the seven-tap half-autocorrelation, with norm (9/8)^d for N >= 7. Levels 1, 2 and 3 remain the exact values (299/256)^d, (9663/8192)^d and (309991/262144)^d for N >= 19, 43 and 91. Bibliographic priority of the closed form is unresolved; see docs/RELATED_WORK.md. A conditional propagation then carries a supplied summary Lipschitz bound and a supplied seminorm comparison through the level-one operator. Bottleneck stability, persistence diagrams and landscape non-expansiveness are hypotheses, not theorems. Those conditional statements are retained in the sources as auxiliaries and are not selected. Nineteen statements are selected. They are parts of this development, not nineteen independent contributions. The exposition of the cascade argument is docs/CASCADE_THEOREM.md.

records.name: ProductCCC.uncountable_delta_system
records.entry_name: Countable cellularity of arbitrary products via finite subproducts
records.doc: An arbitrary product of topological spaces satisfies the countable chain condition (CCC) whenever every finite subproduct does. For nonempty factors this is an equivalence. The proof includes an indexed uncountable delta-system lemma that permits repeated finite supports, and glues compatible cylinders over a finite common root. Arbitrary products of separable spaces are consequently CCC, without a cardinal bound or separation assumptions and allowing empty factors. Continuous-surjection preservation and the discrete-space countability criterion are proved companions. No unrestricted productivity of CCC factors or productively-CCC theorem is asserted.

records.name: Erdos111.countably_colorable_of_linear
records.entry_name: Erdős Problem 111: bipartizing finite subgraphs of uncountably chromatic graphs
records.doc: A Lean proof that for every real C, a graph whose finite subgraphs on m vertices can each be made bipartite by deleting at most Cm edges has countable chromatic number. Hence h_G(n)/n → ∞ for every graph G that is not countably colorable, in particular for every graph of chromatic number ℵ₁. This answers the second question of Erdős Problem 111 in the affirmative.

records.name: Erdos173.erdos_173
records.entry_name: Erdős Problem 173: monochromatic triangles in two-colorings of the plane
records.doc: A Lean proof that in every two-coloring of the plane any three distinct points that are not the vertices of an equilateral triangle, collinear points included, have a monochromatic congruent copy and at most one equilateral side length is missed, so at most one triangle up to congruence, degenerate or not, has no monochromatic copy. Alternating strips show that one equilateral triangle can be missed. This answers Erdős Problem 173 as Bloom states it and settles the conjecture of Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer and Straus that every non-equilateral triangle has a monochromatic copy, collinear triples included; it is new to our knowledge. The step from arbitrary to measurable colorings adapts OpenAI's rigidity theorem for wild character laws, extended here from the algebraic numbers to the algebraic closure of ℚ(x) in ℂ for every real x, and its transfer from proper to weak measurable colorings.

records.name: Erdos408.normal_order_rate
records.entry_name: Erdős Problem 408: distribution of iterated totient heights
records.doc: A Lean proof that the least k with φ_k(n) = 1 has normal order α log n for a constant 1 / log 3 ≤ α ≤ 1 / log 2, with mean-square error O(x (log x)² / (log log x)⁵). This answers the first two questions of Erdős Problem 408. The proof formalizes extensions of Theorems 3.1 and 6.1 of OpenAI's The Poisson-Dirichlet law for prime predecessors, and uses vendored Lean proofs of the zero-free half-plane re s > 7/8 for Dirichlet L-functions (openai/math) and of the weighted dilation graph results (Yao Xu's totient-fibers-lean4).

records.name: FalconerThetaGauge.theorem_one_one
records.entry_name: Falconer's distance problem for stretched logarithmic gauges
records.doc: A Lean 4 formalization of Theorem 1.1 of the supplied October 2026 manuscript: every compact subset of the Euclidean plane with positive Hausdorff measure for the gauge r exp(-(log(1/r))^theta), with 2/3 < theta < 1, has a distance set of positive Lebesgue measure. The proof constructs gauge Frostman probabilities with finite logarithmic critical and Fourier energies, obtains the required radial Orlicz densities, and decomposes the measures into finite-depth regular pieces. Measurable directional tests and smooth masks define actual filtered distance measures with summable removed mass. Quantitative stationary phase, inverse operators, orthogonality, distance linearization, and space splitting prove all four induction recurrences for the actual energies. A weighted finite-tree argument yields summable frequency-shell bounds; Fourier reconstruction gives absolute continuity of a nonzero weighted distance measure and hence the stated positive Lebesgue measure. The target theorem builds without proof holes and uses only the three standard Lean axioms. Source adaptations are recorded under fidelity.

records.name: KuhnPoker.hasValue_one_one
records.entry_name: Kuhn poker: the value −1/18, all optimal strategies, and the solution at every ante and bet
records.doc: A Lean 4 development of Kuhn's simplified two-person poker (Kuhn 1950): three cards 1 < 2 < 3, one dealt to each player with the six deals equiprobable, an ante of a from each player and a single bet of b, player I acting first, the five courses of play of Kuhn's p. 98 with payoffs a (pass-pass, to the higher card), a to II (pass-bet-pass), a + b to the higher card (pass-bet-bet), a to I (bet-pass) and a + b to the higher card (bet-bet). The definitions are built from the game tree: a behaviour strategy of I is a pair of functions on the three cards (the probability of betting first, the probability of calling after passing and facing a bet), one of II likewise (the probability of betting after a pass, the probability of calling a bet); the payoff is the average over the six deals; a strategy guarantees v when it is valid and earns at least v (holds the opponent to at most v) against every valid strategy of the opponent; the game has value v when each player has a strategy guaranteeing v; an equilibrium is a saddle point. For Kuhn's game a = b = 1, kernel-checked: the value is -1/18 (a game has at most one value), an equilibrium exists, every equilibrium pays I exactly -1/18, and a pair is an equilibrium iff each strategy guarantees -1/18; II's optimal strategy is unique at all six information sets (bet after a pass with the 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 1/3, 0, 1; call with probabilities 0, 1/3, 1 - Kuhn's (xi, eta) = (1/3, 1/3) with the four coordinates he removed as superfluous now proved forced); I's optimal strategies are exactly Kuhn's one-parameter family (bet the 1 with probability alpha and fold it, never bet the 2 first and call with it with probability alpha + 1/3, bet the 3 with probability 3 alpha and call with it, for alpha in [0, 1/3], the call with the 3 being unconstrained exactly when 3 alpha = 1, where that information set is unreached); in the normal form with Kuhn's coding of the 27 and 64 pure strategies, his essential 8 x 4 matrix is six times the game matrix, his twelve basic optimal mixed strategies (A)-(L) and II's two guarantee -1/18, and a mixed strategy is optimal iff its realization plan lies on the family (I) or its marginals are II's strategy (II). For every ante a > 0 and bet b > 0 (Kuhn's pp. 102-103, stated there without proof, and the region b > 2a he does not state): the value is -b^2/(6(2a + b)) for b <= a, -b(2a - b)/(6(2a + b)) for a <= b <= 2a and 0 for b >= 2a, with explicit guaranteeing strategies in each case; in Case 3 the calling probability eta with the 2 ranges over [(2a - b)/(2a + b), b/(2a + b)], and the interval printed on p. 102, b/(2a + b) <= eta <= (a + b)/(2a + b), fails at its upper end (at a = 2, b = 3 and eta = 5/7 II's Case 3 strategy does not guarantee the value). Every guarantee is a finite nonnegative-product identity (the gap between the payoff and the value is a sum of products of the opponent's probabilities and their complements with coefficients nonnegative on the case's region: polynomials in a, b and the free parameter, at general stakes built from a, b, 2a + b, a - b, 2a - b, 4a - b, b - 2a and the interval factors (2a + b)eta - (2a - b), b - (2a + b)eta, 2(a - b) - (2a + b)xi, and, in the optimal-set theorems, the slacks of their stated inequalities), and every "only if" is a linear certificate from finitely many pure strategies (the coefficients rationals at a = b = 1 and, at general stakes, polynomials in a, b and the free parameter nonnegative on the case's region); no formal library found by the dated search holds the game. Beyond Kuhn's statements: the two certificate identities are stated as theorems; the equilibria of Kuhn's game are exactly the pairs (kuhnI α k, kuhnII) with α in [0, 1/3], k in [0, 1] and 3α = 1 or k = 1; and at general stakes the optimal sets are determined - I's strategy is unique for b < a (up to the unreached call with the 3) and for a < b <= 2a, is Kuhn's family on the diagonal b = a at every scale, and for b >= 2a never bets the 1 or the 2 first, folds them, and with the 3 is cut out by one inequality (a single strategy at b = 2a; beyond it a two-dimensional set in which I may also bet the 3 first, with probability at most (b - 2a)/b), so Kuhn's one-parameter family is optimal only at b = a; II's strategy is unique on the diagonal at every scale and a segment for b <= a (the bet with the 2 after a pass free in [0, 2(a - b)/(2a + b)], so Kuhn's 'unique optimal mode of behavior' in Case 1 holds in his behaviour parameters only); for a <= b < 2a its bets after a pass are forced, (b/(2a + b), 0, 1), and its calls form a polytope of three inequalities; for b > 2a it never bets the 1 or the 2 after a pass, never calls with them, and calls with the 3 with probability at least 4a/(2a + b), its bet with the 3 free; and on the line b = 2a its optimal set is a five-dimensional polytope (the bet with the 2 after a pass zero and, with bets (p, 0, r) and calls (s, t, w), 2p <= r, s + t <= p, 1 <= t + w, 1 + p + s <= 2w; nine vertices, replayed); at every ante a > 0 and bet b > 0 every equilibrium pays the value and a pair is an equilibrium iff each strategy guarantees it, so the equilibria are exactly the pairs of optimal strategies, on b = 2a explicitly; the corrected Case 3 interval is sharp, and the printed one holds only at its lower end. A second correction, a misprint, is noted in the documentation: p. 101's table gives β = 5/12 for (I) and (J), where p. 100's mixtures and p. 101's own formula give 7/12.

For Kuhn's game a = b = 1, kernel-checked: the value is -1/18 (a game has at most one value), an equilibrium exists, every equilibrium pays I exactly -1/18, and a pair is an equilibrium iff each strategy guarantees -1/18; II's optimal strategy is unique at all six information sets (bet after a pass with the 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 1/3, 0, 1; call with probabilities 0, 1/3, 1 - Kuhn's (xi, eta) = (1/3, 1/3) with the four coordinates he removed as superfluous now proved forced); I's optimal strategies are exactly Kuhn's one-parameter family (bet the 1 with probability alpha and fold it, never bet the 2 first and call with it with probability alpha + 1/3, bet the 3 with probability 3 alpha and call with it, for alpha in [0, 1/3], the call with the 3 being unconstrained exactly when 3 alpha = 1, where that information set is unreached); in the normal form with Kuhn's coding of the 27 and 64 pure strategies, his essential 8 x 4 matrix is six times the game matrix, his twelve basic optimal mixed strategies (A)-(L) and II's two guarantee -1/18, and a mixed strategy is optimal iff its realization plan lies on the family (I) or its marginals are II's strategy (II). For every ante a > 0 and bet b > 0 (Kuhn's pp. 102-103, stated there without proof, and the region b > 2a he does not state): the value is -b^2/(6(2a + b)) for b <= a, -b(2a - b)/(6(2a + b)) for a <= b <= 2a and 0 for b >= 2a, with explicit guaranteeing strategies in each case; in Case 3 the calling probability eta with the 2 ranges over [(2a - b)/(2a + b), b/(2a + b)], and the interval printed on p. 102, b/(2a + b) <= eta <= (a + b)/(2a + b), fails at its upper end (at a = 2, b = 3 and eta = 5/7 II's Case 3 strategy does not guarantee the value). Every guarantee is a finite nonnegative-product identity (the gap between the payoff and the value is a sum of products of the opponent's probabilities and their complements with coefficients nonnegative on the case's region: polynomials in a, b and the free parameter, at general stakes built from a, b, 2a + b, a - b, 2a - b, 4a - b, b - 2a and the interval factors (2a + b)eta - (2a - b), b - (2a + b)eta, 2(a - b) - (2a + b)xi, and, in the optimal-set theorems, the slacks of their stated inequalities), and every "only if" is a linear certificate from finitely many pure strategies (the coefficients rationals at a = b = 1 and, at general stakes, polynomials in a, b and the free parameter nonnegative on the case's region); no formal library found by the dated search holds the game. Beyond Kuhn's statements: the two certificate identities are stated as theorems; the equilibria of Kuhn's game are exactly the pairs (kuhnI α k, kuhnII) with α in [0, 1/3], k in [0, 1] and 3α = 1 or k = 1; and at general stakes the optimal sets are determined - I's strategy is unique for b < a (up to the unreached call with the 3) and for a < b <= 2a, is Kuhn's family on the diagonal b = a at every scale, and for b >= 2a never bets the 1 or the 2 first, folds them, and with the 3 is cut out by one inequality (a single strategy at b = 2a; beyond it a two-dimensional set in which I may also bet the 3 first, with probability at most (b - 2a)/b), so Kuhn's one-parameter family is optimal only at b = a; II's strategy is unique on the diagonal at every scale and a segment for b <= a (the bet with the 2 after a pass free in [0, 2(a - b)/(2a + b)], so Kuhn's 'unique optimal mode of behavior' in Case 1 holds in his behaviour parameters only); for a <= b < 2a its bets after a pass are forced, (b/(2a + b), 0, 1), and its calls form a polytope of three inequalities; for b > 2a it never bets the 1 or the 2 after a pass, never calls with them, and calls with the 3 with probability at least 4a/(2a + b), its bet with the 3 free; and on the line b = 2a its optimal set is a five-dimensional polytope (the bet with the 2 after a pass zero and, with bets (p, 0, r) and calls (s, t, w), 2p <= r, s + t <= p, 1 <= t + w, 1 + p + s <= 2w; nine vertices, replayed); at every ante a > 0 and bet b > 0 every equilibrium pays the value and a pair is an equilibrium iff each strategy guarantees it, so the equilibria are exactly the pairs of optimal strategies, on b = 2a explicitly; the corrected Case 3 interval is sharp, and the printed one holds only at its lower end. A second correction, a misprint, is noted in the documentation: p. 101's table gives β = 5/12 for (I) and (J), where p. 100's mixtures and p. 101's own formula give 7/12.

The definitions are built from the game tree: a behaviour strategy of I is a pair of functions on the three cards (the probability of betting first, the probability of calling after passing and facing a bet), one of II likewise (the probability of betting after a pass, the probability of calling a bet); the payoff is the average over the six deals; a strategy guarantees v when it is valid and earns at least v (holds the opponent to at most v) against every valid strategy of the opponent; the game has value v when each player has a strategy guaranteeing v; an equilibrium is a saddle point. For Kuhn's game a = b = 1, kernel-checked: the value is -1/18 (a game has at most one value), an equilibrium exists, every equilibrium pays I exactly -1/18, and a pair is an equilibrium iff each strategy guarantees -1/18; II's optimal strategy is unique at all six information sets (bet after a pass with the 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 1/3, 0, 1; call with probabilities 0, 1/3, 1 - Kuhn's (xi, eta) = (1/3, 1/3) with the four coordinates he removed as superfluous now proved forced); I's optimal strategies are exactly Kuhn's one-parameter family (bet the 1 with probability alpha and fold it, never bet the 2 first and call with it with probability alpha + 1/3, bet the 3 with probability 3 alpha and call with it, for alpha in [0, 1/3], the call with the 3 being unconstrained exactly when 3 alpha = 1, where that information set is unreached); in the normal form with Kuhn's coding of the 27 and 64 pure strategies, his essential 8 x 4 matrix is six times the game matrix, his twelve basic optimal mixed strategies (A)-(L) and II's two guarantee -1/18, and a mixed strategy is optimal iff its realization plan lies on the family (I) or its marginals are II's strategy (II). For every ante a > 0 and bet b > 0 (Kuhn's pp. 102-103, stated there without proof, and the region b > 2a he does not state): the value is -b^2/(6(2a + b)) for b <= a, -b(2a - b)/(6(2a + b)) for a <= b <= 2a and 0 for b >= 2a, with explicit guaranteeing strategies in each case; in Case 3 the calling probability eta with the 2 ranges over [(2a - b)/(2a + b), b/(2a + b)], and the interval printed on p. 102, b/(2a + b) <= eta <= (a + b)/(2a + b), fails at its upper end (at a = 2, b = 3 and eta = 5/7 II's Case 3 strategy does not guarantee the value). Every guarantee is a finite nonnegative-product identity (the gap between the payoff and the value is a sum of products of the opponent's probabilities and their complements with coefficients nonnegative on the case's region: polynomials in a, b and the free parameter, at general stakes built from a, b, 2a + b, a - b, 2a - b, 4a - b, b - 2a and the interval factors (2a + b)eta - (2a - b), b - (2a + b)eta, 2(a - b) - (2a + b)xi, and, in the optimal-set theorems, the slacks of their stated inequalities), and every "only if" is a linear certificate from finitely many pure strategies (the coefficients rationals at a = b = 1 and, at general stakes, polynomials in a, b and the free parameter nonnegative on the case's region); no formal library found by the dated search holds the game. Beyond Kuhn's statements: the two certificate identities are stated as theorems; the equilibria of Kuhn's game are exactly the pairs (kuhnI α k, kuhnII) with α in [0, 1/3], k in [0, 1] and 3α = 1 or k = 1; and at general stakes the optimal sets are determined - I's strategy is unique for b < a (up to the unreached call with the 3) and for a < b <= 2a, is Kuhn's family on the diagonal b = a at every scale, and for b >= 2a never bets the 1 or the 2 first, folds them, and with the 3 is cut out by one inequality (a single strategy at b = 2a; beyond it a two-dimensional set in which I may also bet the 3 first, with probability at most (b - 2a)/b), so Kuhn's one-parameter family is optimal only at b = a; II's strategy is unique on the diagonal at every scale and a segment for b <= a (the bet with the 2 after a pass free in [0, 2(a - b)/(2a + b)], so Kuhn's 'unique optimal mode of behavior' in Case 1 holds in his behaviour parameters only); for a <= b < 2a its bets after a pass are forced, (b/(2a + b), 0, 1), and its calls form a polytope of three inequalities; for b > 2a it never bets the 1 or the 2 after a pass, never calls with them, and calls with the 3 with probability at least 4a/(2a + b), its bet with the 3 free; and on the line b = 2a its optimal set is a five-dimensional polytope (the bet with the 2 after a pass zero and, with bets (p, 0, r) and calls (s, t, w), 2p <= r, s + t <= p, 1 <= t + w, 1 + p + s <= 2w; nine vertices, replayed); at every ante a > 0 and bet b > 0 every equilibrium pays the value and a pair is an equilibrium iff each strategy guarantees it, so the equilibria are exactly the pairs of optimal strategies, on b = 2a explicitly; the corrected Case 3 interval is sharp, and the printed one holds only at its lower end. A second correction, a misprint, is noted in the documentation: p. 101's table gives β = 5/12 for (I) and (J), where p. 100's mixtures and p. 101's own formula give 7/12.

The definitions are built from the game tree: a behaviour strategy of I is a pair of functions on the three cards (the probability of betting first, the probability of calling after passing and facing a bet), one of II likewise (the probability of betting after a pass, the probability of calling a bet); the payoff is the average over the six deals; a strategy guarantees v when it is valid and earns at least v (holds the opponent to at most v) against every valid strategy of the opponent; the game has value v when each player has a strategy guaranteeing v; an equilibrium is a saddle point. For Kuhn's game a = b = 1, kernel-checked: the value is -1/18 (a game has at most one value), an equilibrium exists, every equilibrium pays I exactly -1/18, and a pair is an equilibrium iff each strategy guarantees -1/18; II's optimal strategy is unique at all six information sets (bet after a pass with the 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 1/3, 0, 1; call with probabilities 0, 1/3, 1 - Kuhn's (xi, eta) = (1/3, 1/3) with the four coordinates he removed as superfluous now proved forced); I's optimal strategies are exactly Kuhn's one-parameter family (bet the 1 with probability alpha and fold it, never bet the 2 first and call with it with probability alpha + 1/3, bet the 3 with probability 3 alpha and call with it, for alpha in [0, 1/3], the call with the 3 being unconstrained exactly when 3 alpha = 1, where that information set is unreached); in the normal form with Kuhn's coding of the 27 and 64 pure strategies, his essential 8 x 4 matrix is six times the game matrix, his twelve basic optimal mixed strategies (A)-(L) and II's two guarantee -1/18, and a mixed strategy is optimal iff its realization plan lies on the family (I) or its marginals are II's strategy (II). For every ante a > 0 and bet b > 0 (Kuhn's pp. 102-103, stated there without proof, and the region b > 2a he does not state): the value is -b^2/(6(2a + b)) for b <= a, -b(2a - b)/(6(2a + b)) for a <= b <= 2a and 0 for b >= 2a, with explicit guaranteeing strategies in each case; in Case 3 the calling probability eta with the 2 ranges over [(2a - b)/(2a + b), b/(2a + b)], and the interval printed on p. 102, b/(2a + b) <= eta <= (a + b)/(2a + b), fails at its upper end (at a = 2, b = 3 and eta = 5/7 II's Case 3 strategy does not guarantee the value). Every guarantee is a finite nonnegative-product identity (the gap between the payoff and the value is a sum of products of the opponent's probabilities and their complements with coefficients nonnegative on the case's region: polynomials in a, b and the free parameter, at general stakes built from a, b, 2a + b, a - b, 2a - b, 4a - b, b - 2a and the interval factors (2a + b)eta - (2a - b), b - (2a + b)eta, 2(a - b) - (2a + b)xi, and, in the optimal-set theorems, the slacks of their stated inequalities), and every "only if" is a linear certificate from finitely many pure strategies (the coefficients rationals at a = b = 1 and, at general stakes, polynomials in a, b and the free parameter nonnegative on the case's region); no formal library found by the dated search holds the game. Beyond Kuhn's statements: the two certificate identities are stated as theorems; the equilibria of Kuhn's game are exactly the pairs (kuhnI α k, kuhnII) with α in [0, 1/3], k in [0, 1] and 3α = 1 or k = 1; and at general stakes the optimal sets are determined - I's strategy is unique for b < a (up to the unreached call with the 3) and for a < b <= 2a, is Kuhn's family on the diagonal b = a at every scale, and for b >= 2a never bets the 1 or the 2 first, folds them, and with the 3 is cut out by one inequality (a single strategy at b = 2a; beyond it a two-dimensional set in which I may also bet the 3 first, with probability at most (b - 2a)/b), so Kuhn's one-parameter family is optimal only at b = a; II's strategy is unique on the diagonal at every scale and a segment for b <= a (the bet with the 2 after a pass free in [0, 2(a - b)/(2a + b)], so Kuhn's 'unique optimal mode of behavior' in Case 1 holds in his behaviour parameters only); for a <= b < 2a its bets after a pass are forced, (b/(2a + b), 0, 1), and its calls form a polytope of three inequalities; for b > 2a it never bets the 1 or the 2 after a pass, never calls with them, and calls with the 3 with probability at least 4a/(2a + b), its bet with the 3 free; and on the line b = 2a its optimal set is a five-dimensional polytope (the bet with the 2 after a pass zero and, with bets (p, 0, r) and calls (s, t, w), 2p <= r, s + t <= p, 1 <= t + w, 1 + p + s <= 2w; nine vertices, replayed); at every ante a > 0 and bet b > 0 every equilibrium pays the value and a pair is an equilibrium iff each strategy guarantees it, so the equilibria are exactly the pairs of optimal strategies, on b = 2a explicitly; the corrected Case 3 interval is sharp, and the printed one holds only at its lower end. A second correction, a misprint, is noted in the documentation: p. 101's table gives β = 5/12 for (I) and (J), where p. 100's mixtures and p. 101's own formula give 7/12.

The definitions are built from the game tree: a behaviour strategy of I is a pair of functions on the three cards (the probability of betting first, the probability of calling after passing and facing a bet), one of II likewise (the probability of betting after a pass, the probability of calling a bet); the payoff is the average over the six deals; a strategy guarantees v when it is valid and earns at least v (holds the opponent to at most v) against every valid strategy of the opponent; the game has value v when each player has a strategy guaranteeing v; an equilibrium is a saddle point. For Kuhn's game a = b = 1, kernel-checked: the value is -1/18 (a game has at most one value), an equilibrium exists, every equilibrium pays I exactly -1/18, and a pair is an equilibrium iff each strategy guarantees -1/18; II's optimal strategy is unique at all six information sets (bet after a pass with the 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 1/3, 0, 1; call with probabilities 0, 1/3, 1 - Kuhn's (xi, eta) = (1/3, 1/3) with the four coordinates he removed as superfluous now proved forced); I's optimal strategies are exactly Kuhn's one-parameter family (bet the 1 with probability alpha and fold it, never bet the 2 first and call with it with probability alpha + 1/3, bet the 3 with probability 3 alpha and call with it, for alpha in [0, 1/3], the call with the 3 being unconstrained exactly when 3 alpha = 1, where that information set is unreached); in the normal form with Kuhn's coding of the 27 and 64 pure strategies, his essential 8 x 4 matrix is six times the game matrix, his twelve basic optimal mixed strategies (A)-(L) and II's two guarantee -1/18, and a mixed strategy is optimal iff its realization plan lies on the family (I) or its marginals are II's strategy (II). For every ante a > 0 and bet b > 0 (Kuhn's pp. 102-103, stated there without proof, and the region b > 2a he does not state): the value is -b^2/(6(2a + b)) for b <= a, -b(2a - b)/(6(2a + b)) for a <= b <= 2a and 0 for b >= 2a, with explicit guaranteeing strategies in each case; in Case 3 the calling probability eta with the 2 ranges over [(2a - b)/(2a + b), b/(2a + b)], and the interval printed on p. 102, b/(2a + b) <= eta <= (a + b)/(2a + b), fails at its upper end (at a = 2, b = 3 and eta = 5/7 II's Case 3 strategy does not guarantee the value). Every guarantee is a finite nonnegative-product identity (the gap between the payoff and the value is a sum of products of the opponent's probabilities and their complements with coefficients nonnegative on the case's region: polynomials in a, b and the free parameter, at general stakes built from a, b, 2a + b, a - b, 2a - b, 4a - b, b - 2a and the interval factors (2a + b)eta - (2a - b), b - (2a + b)eta, 2(a - b) - (2a + b)xi, and, in the optimal-set theorems, the slacks of their stated inequalities), and every "only if" is a linear certificate from finitely many pure strategies (the coefficients rationals at a = b = 1 and, at general stakes, polynomials in a, b and the free parameter nonnegative on the case's region); no formal library found by the dated search holds the game. Beyond Kuhn's statements: the two certificate identities are stated as theorems; the equilibria of Kuhn's game are exactly the pairs (kuhnI α k, kuhnII) with α in [0, 1/3], k in [0, 1] and 3α = 1 or k = 1; and at general stakes the optimal sets are determined - I's strategy is unique for b < a (up to the unreached call with the 3) and for a < b <= 2a, is Kuhn's family on the diagonal b = a at every scale, and for b >= 2a never bets the 1 or the 2 first, folds them, and with the 3 is cut out by one inequality (a single strategy at b = 2a; beyond it a two-dimensional set in which I may also bet the 3 first, with probability at most (b - 2a)/b), so Kuhn's one-parameter family is optimal only at b = a; II's strategy is unique on the diagonal at every scale and a segment for b <= a (the bet with the 2 after a pass free in [0, 2(a - b)/(2a + b)], so Kuhn's 'unique optimal mode of behavior' in Case 1 holds in his behaviour parameters only); for a <= b < 2a its bets after a pass are forced, (b/(2a + b), 0, 1), and its calls form a polytope of three inequalities; for b > 2a it never bets the 1 or the 2 after a pass, never calls with them, and calls with the 3 with probability at least 4a/(2a + b), its bet with the 3 free; and on the line b = 2a its optimal set is a five-dimensional polytope (the bet with the 2 after a pass zero and, with bets (p, 0, r) and calls (s, t, w), 2p <= r, s + t <= p, 1 <= t + w, 1 + p + s <= 2w; nine vertices, replayed); at every ante a > 0 and bet b > 0 every equilibrium pays the value and a pair is an equilibrium iff each strategy guarantees it, so the equilibria are exactly the pairs of optimal strategies, on b = 2a explicitly; the corrected Case 3 interval is sharp, and the printed one holds only at its lower end. A second correction, a misprint, is noted in the documentation: p. 101's table gives β = 5/12 for (I) and (J), where p. 100's mixtures and p. 101's own formula give 7/12.

The definitions are built from the game tree: a behaviour strategy of I is a pair of functions on the three cards (the probability of betting first, the probability of calling after passing and facing a bet), one of II likewise (the probability of betting after a pass, the probability of calling a bet); the payoff is the average over the six deals; a strategy guarantees v when it is valid and earns at least v (holds the opponent to at most v) against every valid strategy of the opponent; the game has value v when each player has a strategy guaranteeing v; an equilibrium is a saddle point. For Kuhn's game a = b = 1, kernel-checked: the value is -1/18 (a game has at most one value), an equilibrium exists, every equilibrium pays I exactly -1/18, and a pair is an equilibrium iff each strategy guarantees -1/18; II's optimal strategy is unique at all six information sets (bet after a pass with the 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 1/3, 0, 1; call with probabilities 0, 1/3, 1 - Kuhn's (xi, eta) = (1/3, 1/3) with the four coordinates he removed as superfluous now proved forced); I's optimal strategies are exactly Kuhn's one-parameter family (bet the 1 with probability alpha and fold it, never bet the 2 first and call with it with probability alpha + 1/3, bet the 3 with probability 3 alpha and call with it, for alpha in [0, 1/3], the call with the 3 being unconstrained exactly when 3 alpha = 1, where that information set is unreached); in the normal form with Kuhn's coding of the 27 and 64 pure strategies, his essential 8 x 4 matrix is six times the game matrix, his twelve basic optimal mixed strategies (A)-(L) and II's two guarantee -1/18, and a mixed strategy is optimal iff its realization plan lies on the family (I) or its marginals are II's strategy (II). For every ante a > 0 and bet b > 0 (Kuhn's pp. 102-103, stated there without proof, and the region b > 2a he does not state): the value is -b^2/(6(2a + b)) for b <= a, -b(2a - b)/(6(2a + b)) for a <= b <= 2a and 0 for b >= 2a, with explicit guaranteeing strategies in each case; in Case 3 the calling probability eta with the 2 ranges over [(2a - b)/(2a + b), b/(2a + b)], and the interval printed on p. 102, b/(2a + b) <= eta <= (a + b)/(2a + b), fails at its upper end (at a = 2, b = 3 and eta = 5/7 II's Case 3 strategy does not guarantee the value). Every guarantee is a finite nonnegative-product identity (the gap between the payoff and the value is a sum of products of the opponent's probabilities and their complements with coefficients nonnegative on the case's region: polynomials in a, b and the free parameter, at general stakes built from a, b, 2a + b, a - b, 2a - b, 4a - b, b - 2a and the interval factors (2a + b)eta - (2a - b), b - (2a + b)eta, 2(a - b) - (2a + b)xi, and, in the optimal-set theorems, the slacks of their stated inequalities), and every "only if" is a linear certificate from finitely many pure strategies (the coefficients rationals at a = b = 1 and, at general stakes, polynomials in a, b and the free parameter nonnegative on the case's region); no formal library found by the dated search holds the game. Beyond Kuhn's statements: the two certificate identities are stated as theorems; the equilibria of Kuhn's game are exactly the pairs (kuhnI α k, kuhnII) with α in [0, 1/3], k in [0, 1] and 3α = 1 or k = 1; and at general stakes the optimal sets are determined - I's strategy is unique for b < a (up to the unreached call with the 3) and for a < b <= 2a, is Kuhn's family on the diagonal b = a at every scale, and for b >= 2a never bets the 1 or the 2 first, folds them, and with the 3 is cut out by one inequality (a single strategy at b = 2a; beyond it a two-dimensional set in which I may also bet the 3 first, with probability at most (b - 2a)/b), so Kuhn's one-parameter family is optimal only at b = a; II's strategy is unique on the diagonal at every scale and a segment for b <= a (the bet with the 2 after a pass free in [0, 2(a - b)/(2a + b)], so Kuhn's 'unique optimal mode of behavior' in Case 1 holds in his behaviour parameters only); for a <= b < 2a its bets after a pass are forced, (b/(2a + b), 0, 1), and its calls form a polytope of three inequalities; for b > 2a it never bets the 1 or the 2 after a pass, never calls with them, and calls with the 3 with probability at least 4a/(2a + b), its bet with the 3 free; and on the line b = 2a its optimal set is a five-dimensional polytope (the bet with the 2 after a pass zero and, with bets (p, 0, r) and calls (s, t, w), 2p <= r, s + t <= p, 1 <= t + w, 1 + p + s <= 2w; nine vertices, replayed); at every ante a > 0 and bet b > 0 every equilibrium pays the value and a pair is an equilibrium iff each strategy guarantees it, so the equilibria are exactly the pairs of optimal strategies, on b = 2a explicitly; the corrected Case 3 interval is sharp, and the printed one holds only at its lower end. A second correction, a misprint, is noted in the documentation: p. 101's table gives β = 5/12 for (I) and (J), where p. 100's mixtures and p. 101's own formula give 7/12.

records.name: OrientationColouring.alon_tarsi
records.entry_name: The Alon–Tarsi theorem and 3-choosability of planar bipartite graphs
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of the Alon–Tarsi theorem: if a finite simple graph has an orientation whose numbers of even and odd Eulerian subdigraphs differ, then it can be properly coloured from any lists larger than the out-degrees; and of its corollary that every finite planar bipartite graph is 3-choosable. Planarity is the combinatorial notion of a plane map (a rotation system of genus zero) of the registered entry PALOMAR-2026-10-15-000005, whose definitions are reproduced verbatim in the Challenge. The proof uses the graph polynomial and Mathlib's Combinatorial Nullstellensatz, Euler's formula for plane maps, and an out-degree-2 orientation obtained from Hall's theorem.

records.name: OddBarker.odd_length_mem
records.entry_name: Barker sequences of odd length have length 1, 3, 5, 7, 11 or 13
records.doc: A Lean 4 development of the classification of Barker sequences of odd length. A Barker sequence of length n is a sequence h of n signs whose aperiodic autocorrelations C(k), the sum over j < n - k of h(j) h(j + k), satisfy |C(k)| <= 1 for 0 < k < n. Turyn and Storer (1961) stated, and gave a proof, that a Barker sequence of odd length n > 1 has length 3, 5, 7, 11 or 13 (length 1 is admitted here: it has no nontrivial shift). Theorem 1(iv) of Turyn–Storer, on which their proof relies, is false as stated (Willms 2014, explicit counterexamples); per Schmidt–Willms (footnote 1) parts (ii) and (iii) imply (iv) on a corrected range that suffices for the induction, and independent proofs exist (Borwein–Erdélyi 2013; Schmidt–Willms 2016, the proof formalized here). The proof formalized is that of Schmidt and Willms (2016), recast so that the classification needs no enumeration of sequences: for odd n and m = (n - 1)/2, odd shifts have autocorrelation 0 and even shifts (-1)^m (from C(u) + C(n - u) = n mod 4); skew-symmetry h(k) h(n - 1 - k) = (-1)^(m + k); the folded identity, the sum over k <= w of (-1)^k h(k) h(w - k), equals 1 for every even w <= n - 3; the doubling law h(u - 1) h(u) = h(2u - 1) h(2u) for 1 <= u <= (n - 3)/2; Schmidt and Willms's Lemmas 3 and 4 in sign-change form (for n >= 7 and h(0) = h(1), with p the first sign change and q the first sign change not divisible by p, both are odd and 2q - 3 <= n <= p + q + 1, Lemma 4 by one generating-function identity for the folded sums); and an endgame that leaves n in {7, 11, 13}, excluding n = 9 by skew-symmetry and doubling, with the alternation h(j) -> (-1)^j h(j) for the normalization h(0) = h(1). Eight witnesses, one at each length 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 11 and 13, are Barker by decide, and every Barker sequence of odd length equals a fixed sequence of its length (canon) up to negation and alternation, by a kernel enumeration of the 2^n sign patterns at each of the six odd lengths. Also proved: the even reduction of Turyn and Storer's footnote 2, that a Barker sequence of even length n > 2 has 4 | n and yields a real circulant Hadamard matrix of order n. Given the even-length classification as an explicit hypothesis (every Barker sequence of positive even length has length 2 or 4, the statement even_length_eq_two_or_four of openai/math, family 179), a Barker sequence of positive length n exists exactly when n is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 11 or 13, and every Barker sequence has length at most 13; the same follows from the hypothesis that real circulant Hadamard matrices of positive order exist only at orders 1 and 4 (the forward direction of exists_iff_order_one_or_four of openai/math), through the even reduction. The seven definitions are restated from openai/math's two challenge files, character for character except the two Fin-bound proofs inside aperiodic (explicit terms in place of by omega, which under the module system yields module-private auxiliary theorems the comparator rejects), so its two theorems discharge the hypotheses, even_length_eq_two_or_four by unfolding alone and exists_iff_order_one_or_four by unfolding and Iff.mp; they are not proved here. records.name: ContinuedFractionBounds.convergent_eq
records.entry_name: Sharp continued-fraction bounds from exact digit runs
records.doc: Proves sharp bounds for both extrema of three consecutive ordinary continued-fraction approximation coefficients. Exact finite runs of every integer central digit at least two have rational four-corner constants, unique coordinate extremizers, strict actual inequalities, and optimality within the prescribed digit classes. The project also proves exact clipping on every closed unit-square rectangle for every real parameter at least one; sharp inverse stability for both extrema for every real parameter at least two, including their equality loci and actual-convergent optimality; fixed-word sharpness at a fixed index; constant-future and exhausted-past boundary results; effective two-sided run-gap estimates; optimal actual constant-digit-window cutoffs; and an executable rational Lean interface.

records.doc: Proves sharp bounds for both extrema of three consecutive ordinary continued-fraction approximation coefficients. Exact finite runs of every integer central digit at least two have rational four-corner constants, unique coordinate extremizers, strict actual inequalities, and optimality within the prescribed digit classes. The project also proves exact clipping on every closed unit-square rectangle for every real parameter at least one; sharp inverse stability for both extrema for every real parameter at least two, including their equality loci and actual-convergent optimality; fixed-word sharpness at a fixed index; constant-future and exhausted-past boundary results; effective two-sided run-gap estimates; optimal actual constant-digit-window cutoffs; and an executable rational Lean interface.

records.name: TriangleNumerical.entropy_certificate
records.entry_name: A certificate for the triangle variational problem
records.doc:
A Lean formalization of a technical lemma in the paper "Nonlinear lower-tail large deviations at criticality" by Matthew Kwan and Huy Tuan Pham. This lemma is used to solve a certain variational problem, which is necessary to characterise the probability that a random graph is triangle-free in the so-called "critical regime" where the edge probability is of order 1 / sqrt n.
Specifically, this lemma defines a "certificate function" G and proves that it satisfies a certain inequality. This involves lots of interval arithmetic.

records.name: BergmanWeakType.projection_constant_eq_one
records.entry_name: Bergman projection weak type constants
records.doc: A Lean formalization of weak type (1,1) constants for the Bergman projection and its positive-kernel counterpart on the unit disk. The proved results are the sharp unweighted constants, weighted positive-kernel constants, and upper and lower weighted bounds for the complex projection. A further theorem characterizes Euclidean disks among bounded simply connected open regions using their reproducing Bergman kernels, without boundary regularity assumptions. All seven main comparison targets are proved using only the standard permitted Lean axioms.

The proved results are the sharp unweighted constants, weighted positive-kernel constants, and upper and lower weighted bounds for the complex projection. A further theorem characterizes Euclidean disks among bounded simply connected open regions using their reproducing Bergman kernels, without boundary regularity assumptions. All seven main comparison targets are proved using only the standard permitted Lean axioms.

records.name: TrilinearHT.trilinear_ht_bound
records.entry_name: Formalization of L^3 boundedness of the trilinear Hilbert transform
records.doc: This is a Lean 4 formalization of the `L³ x L³ x L³ → L¹` boundedness of the trilinear Hilbert transform. The formalization follows a blueprint that was generated by GPT-6 Astra Pro on the basis of a  preprint claiming this result made public by OpenAI on Oct 6, 2026, and of a revised, shorter version of its argument generated by GPT-6. The preprint was made public without an accompanying formalization leaving possible  doubts about its correctness. This formalization formally verifies its main result. The theorem statement is human-written, while the proof was autoformalized by coding agents.

records.name: KuratowskiUlam.hasCountablePiBase_of_secondCountable
records.entry_name: Kuratowski–Ulam category theorem for countable pi-base spaces
records.doc: For arbitrary topological spaces X and Y, if Y has a countable pi-base, a nowhere dense subset of X × Y has nowhere dense vertical sections outside a meagre subset of X. Meagre subsets likewise have meagre sections for residually many parameters, and residual subsets have residual sections. No Baire, separation or nonemptiness assumption is required for these forward results. For sets with the property of Baire, assuming both factors are Baire, meagreness and residuality are each equivalent to the corresponding generic section property. The product of two Baire spaces is consequently Baire when the second factor has a countable pi-base. Empty spaces and independent type universes are included. Classical mathematics; no novelty or priority claimed.

records.name: CyclePacking.erdos_posa
records.entry_name: The Erdős–Pósa theorem for cycles
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of the Erdős–Pósa theorem: for every k, every finite simple graph either contains k vertex-disjoint cycles or has a set of at most c (k + 1)(log₂(k + 1) + 1) vertices meeting every cycle, for a fixed constant c (the proof gives c = 65); together with the qualitative Erdős–Pósa property and the easy converse that a feedback vertex set of size s rules out s + 1 disjoint cycles. Mathlib has acyclic graphs but not this theorem.

records.name: LovaszLocalLemma.lll
records.entry_name: The Lovász Local Lemma and two applications
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of the Lovász Local Lemma for finitely many events in a probability space with a dependency graph (each event mutually independent, in the sense of Mathlib's `ProbabilityTheory.Indep` of generated σ-algebras, of its non-neighbours), in its general form (P(A_i) ≤ x_i ∏_{j∼i}(1 − x_j) implies P(no event) ≥ ∏(1 − x_i)) and its symmetric form (e p (d + 1) ≤ 1 implies P(no event) > 0); and of two applications: Spencer's Ramsey lower bound (if 2e(C(k,2)C(n,k−2) + 1) ≤ 2^C(k,2) then R(k,k) > n) and the Erdős–Lovász property B theorem for k-uniform hypergraphs (each edge meeting at most d others with e(d + 1) ≤ 2^(k−1); and the case where every vertex lies in at most k edges, for k ≥ 9). Mathlib has independence and product measures but not the Local Lemma.

records.name: DedekindSubgroups.theorem_1_1
records.entry_name: DedekindSubgroups: a congruence modulo 16 for sums of Dedekind sums over subgroups of odd order
records.doc: For k >= 2 and a subgroup H of odd order n of the unit group (Z/kZ)^x, the sum S(H,k) of the Dedekind sums s(h,k) over h in H satisfies: 12k S(H,k) is an integer congruent to n(k-1)(k-2) modulo 16, and the modulus 16 cannot be replaced by 32 (an explicit pair of order-3 subgroups of (Z/63Z)^x). The development also proves a congruence modulo 8 for every subgroup, a congruence for 2k S(H,k) when 3 does not divide k, and, for primes p > 3 and n > 1, that 2S(H,p) is an integer congruent to n(p-1)/2 modulo 8, which refines Louboutin's parity theorem and gives 12S(H,p) - p congruent to 3n(p-1) - p modulo 48. The proof formalizes Meyer's formula 12k s(h,k) = (k-1)(k-2) - 4I(h,k), where I(h,k) counts the inversions of x -> hx mod k, and the facts that these inversion counts are even on squares and equal for inverse elements.

records.name: KneserTheorem.octahedral_tucker
records.entry_name: Kneser's conjecture and the octahedral Tucker lemma
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of Lovász's theorem (Kneser's conjecture): for 0 < k and 2k ≤ n the Kneser graph KG(n, k) of k-subsets of an n-set, adjacent when disjoint, has chromatic number exactly n − 2k + 2; proved combinatorially from the octahedral Tucker lemma (an antipodal labelling of the nonzero sign vectors of length n by nonzero integers in [−m, m] with m < n has a complementary pair x ≼ y with λ(x) = −λ(y)), which is itself proved by Ky Fan's parity argument. Mathlib has neither Kneser graphs nor Tucker's lemma.

records.name: NormalizerLean.isHStar_one
records.entry_name: The normalizer of Γ_Δ(N) for every N and every Δ
records.doc: Formal statements and proofs, in Lean 4 with Mathlib, about the normalizer in SL₂(ℝ) of Γ_Δ(N) for every N ≥ 1 and every subgroup Δ ≤ (ℤ/N)ˣ, with or without −1. Let h* be the largest h with h² ∣ N, d² ≡ 1 (mod h) for every d ∈ Δ, and Δ ⊇ ker((ℤ/N)ˣ → (ℤ/(N/h))ˣ); let n* = N/h*² and D* = diag(h*, 1). Then D*⁻¹Γ₀(n*)D* ≤ Nor(Γ_Δ(N)) ≤ D*⁻¹Γ₀(n*)⁺D*; an Atkin–Lehner element w_Q of level n* (conjugated by D*) normalizes Γ_Δ(N) iff ι*_Q(Δ̄) = Δ̄, where ι*_Q inverts the components of (ℤ/(N/h*))ˣ at the primes of Q; so Nor(Γ_Δ(N)) is described exactly, its index over Γ_Δ(N) is [(ℤ/N)ˣ : Δ]·ψ(N)/ψ(n*)·#{Q ∥ n* : ι*_Q(Δ̄) = Δ̄}, and Nor(Γ_Δ(N)) ≤ Nor(Γ₀(N)) iff h* ∣ h(N). This is Zemel's determination of these normalizers, restated in closed form. 20 theorems, no sorry, only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

records.name: BanachMazur.exists_compatiblePlay
records.entry_name: Oxtoby's Banach–Mazur characterization of Baire spaces
records.doc: An arbitrary topological space is Baire if and only if the first player has no winning full-history strategy in the nested nonempty-open Banach–Mazur game. The proof constructs a compatible play with one common point from disjoint dense response levels, and constructs a winning strategy from failure of Baireness. It separately verifies compatible-play existence, equality of the two players’ intersections and the empty-space boundary. No separation, countability or metric hypothesis is imposed. This is classical mathematics, not a novelty or determinacy claim.

records.doc: An arbitrary topological space is Baire if and only if the first player has no winning full-history strategy in the nested nonempty-open Banach–Mazur game. The proof constructs a compatible play with one common point from disjoint dense response levels, and constructs a winning strategy from failure of Baireness. It separately verifies compatible-play existence, equality of the two players’ intersections and the empty-space boundary. No separation, countability or metric hypothesis is imposed. This is classical mathematics, not a novelty or determinacy claim.

records.name: ChoquetProduct.follows_intersection_eq
records.entry_name: The Baire product theorem for Choquet spaces
records.doc: An arbitrary Baire topological space times a space with a winning full-history second-player Banach–Mazur strategy is Baire. A disjoint dense rectangle tree yields, for each prescribed nonempty open fiber region, a dense Gδ set of parameters with a common-point fiber witness for every countable dense-open product family. An explicit shrinking-ball strategy establishes alpha-favorability of complete metric spaces. Empty factors and legal-play existence are treated explicitly. This is classical mathematics, not a novelty or determinacy claim.

records.name: FixedOrderFactor.muAvg_eq
records.entry_name: FixedOrderFactor: the order-r correction factor for mean squares of L(1, chi), and the factor 35/34
records.doc: For an integer r >= 2 and a finite set N of primes, the random Euler product model for Dirichlet characters of order r replaces chi(q) by independent uniform r-th roots of unity. The development proves that the order-r local factor E|1 - z/q|^(-2) equals (1 + q^-r)/((1 - q^-2)(1 - q^-r)), that its ratio to the full-circle factor (1 - q^-2)^(-1), multiplied over the primes outside N, is zeta^(N)(r)^2 / zeta^(N)(2r), that this correction factor is also the sum of (ab)^-r over the coprime pairs of integers prime to N, and that the model mean is zeta^(N)(2) zeta^(N)(r)^2 / zeta^(N)(2r). The factor exceeds 1, decreases strictly in r and tends to 1; for r = 2k and N empty it equals -binom(4k,2k) B_{2k}^2/(2 B_{4k}). For r = 4 and N = {2} it is 35/34, the ratio by which the limit of Louboutin's mean square of L(1, chi) with the factor at 2 removed changes when the average is restricted to quartic characters; with the forced factor 4/5 at 2 the development also proves the constants pi^2/10, 7 pi^2/68, 7 pi^2/36 and 7/136 = (1/20)(35/34) = (7/72)(9/17). It also identifies the pairs the model keeps: for positive m, n the average of z^m conj(z^n) is 1 exactly when m/n is an r-th power in Q, that is when (m, n) = (d a^r, d b^r) with a, b coprime, and 0 otherwise. Modulo a single prime p with r | p - 1 it proves the finite-character counterpart: there are exactly r Dirichlet characters mod p with chi^r = 1, the sum of chi(a) conj(chi(b)) over them is r when a/b is a nonzero r-th power mod p and 0 otherwise, so every pair (d a^r, d b^r) prime to p survives with sum r; by contrast, summed over all characters mod p, chi(m) conj(chi(n)) has sum 0 for distinct m, n < p.

records.name: NormalizerLean.isUnit_det_of_mem_normG_inf
records.entry_name: Normalizers of congruence subgroups at mixed level: Γ_{H₁}(N₁) ∩ Γ_{H₂}(N₂)
records.doc: Formal statements and proofs, in Lean 4 with Mathlib, about the normalizer in SL₂(ℝ) of Γ = Γ_{H₁}(N₁) ∩ Γ_{H₂}(N₂) for coprime N₁ and N₂, the group of the fibre product X_{H₁} ×_{X(1)} X_{H₂}, where H₁ ≤ SL₂(ℤ/N₁) is such that, at every p ∣ N₁, H₁ mod p fixes no line or H₁ mod p^{v_p(N₁)} lies in a split Cartan subgroup, and H₂ ≤ SL₂(ℤ/N₂) is arbitrary. Nor(Γ) ≤ Nor(Γ_{H₂}(N₂)); an element (det m)^{−1/2}·m of Nor(Γ_{H₂}(N₂)) normalizes Γ iff m mod N₁ normalizes H₁; and |Nor(Γ)/Γ| is [N(H₁) : H₁] times the number of classes of Nor(Γ_{H₂})/Γ_{H₂} whose determinant mod N₁ is the determinant of an element of the normalizer of H₁ in GL₂(ℤ/N₁). Explicit forms follow for Γ_Δ(N₂) (the class of an Atkin–Lehner involution w_Q contains an element of Nor(Γ) iff Q mod N₁ is such a determinant) and for H₂ of prime level fixing exactly one line; corollaries for Γ(N₁), Γ_ns⁺(p) and Γ_sp⁺(p); and an example: for the quaternion group Q₈ ≤ SL₂(F₇), the determinants are the squares, and Γ_{Q₈}(7) ∩ Γ₀(3) has 6 modular automorphisms, not 12, because the Fricke involution of X₀(3) does not lift. 18 theorems, no sorry, only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

records.doc: Formal statements and proofs, in Lean 4 with Mathlib, about the normalizer in SL₂(ℝ) of Γ = Γ_{H₁}(N₁) ∩ Γ_{H₂}(N₂) for coprime N₁ and N₂, the group of the fibre product X_{H₁} ×_{X(1)} X_{H₂}, where H₁ ≤ SL₂(ℤ/N₁) is such that, at every p ∣ N₁, H₁ mod p fixes no line or H₁ mod p^{v_p(N₁)} lies in a split Cartan subgroup, and H₂ ≤ SL₂(ℤ/N₂) is arbitrary. Nor(Γ) ≤ Nor(Γ_{H₂}(N₂)); an element (det m)^{−1/2}·m of Nor(Γ_{H₂}(N₂)) normalizes Γ iff m mod N₁ normalizes H₁; and |Nor(Γ)/Γ| is [N(H₁) : H₁] times the number of classes of Nor(Γ_{H₂})/Γ_{H₂} whose determinant mod N₁ is the determinant of an element of the normalizer of H₁ in GL₂(ℤ/N₁). Explicit forms follow for Γ_Δ(N₂) (the class of an Atkin–Lehner involution w_Q contains an element of Nor(Γ) iff Q mod N₁ is such a determinant) and for H₂ of prime level fixing exactly one line; corollaries for Γ(N₁), Γ_ns⁺(p) and Γ_sp⁺(p); and an example: for the quaternion group Q₈ ≤ SL₂(F₇), the determinants are the squares, and Γ_{Q₈}(7) ∩ Γ₀(3) has 6 modular automorphisms, not 12, because the Fricke involution of X₀(3) does not lift. 18 theorems, no sorry, only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

records.doc: Formal statements and proofs, in Lean 4 with Mathlib, about the normalizer in SL₂(ℝ) of Γ = Γ_{H₁}(N₁) ∩ Γ_{H₂}(N₂) for coprime N₁ and N₂, the group of the fibre product X_{H₁} ×_{X(1)} X_{H₂}, where H₁ ≤ SL₂(ℤ/N₁) is such that, at every p ∣ N₁, H₁ mod p fixes no line or H₁ mod p^{v_p(N₁)} lies in a split Cartan subgroup, and H₂ ≤ SL₂(ℤ/N₂) is arbitrary. Nor(Γ) ≤ Nor(Γ_{H₂}(N₂)); an element (det m)^{−1/2}·m of Nor(Γ_{H₂}(N₂)) normalizes Γ iff m mod N₁ normalizes H₁; and |Nor(Γ)/Γ| is [N(H₁) : H₁] times the number of classes of Nor(Γ_{H₂})/Γ_{H₂} whose determinant mod N₁ is the determinant of an element of the normalizer of H₁ in GL₂(ℤ/N₁). Explicit forms follow for Γ_Δ(N₂) (the class of an Atkin–Lehner involution w_Q contains an element of Nor(Γ) iff Q mod N₁ is such a determinant) and for H₂ of prime level fixing exactly one line; corollaries for Γ(N₁), Γ_ns⁺(p) and Γ_sp⁺(p); and an example: for the quaternion group Q₈ ≤ SL₂(F₇), the determinants are the squares, and Γ_{Q₈}(7) ∩ Γ₀(3) has 6 modular automorphisms, not 12, because the Fricke involution of X₀(3) does not lift. 18 theorems, no sorry, only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

records.name: JinTheorem.jin
records.entry_name: Jin's theorem on dense triangle-free graphs
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of Jin's theorem: a finite triangle-free graph on n vertices with minimum degree greater than 10n/29 is 3-colourable; and of its sharpness: for every m ≥ 1 the blow-up of the Grötzsch graph with weights 3m, 2m, 4m is a triangle-free 10m-regular graph on 29m vertices that is not 3-colourable (Häggkvist). This extends the case r = 2 of the Andrásfai–Erdős–Sós theorem, which is in Mathlib. Mathlib does not have Jin's theorem.

records.name: SteeringWord.tendsto_complexity_div
records.entry_name: Stephan 2026: superlinear complexity of the (3/2)^n steering word
records.doc: A minimal Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of R. Stephan, Superlinear complexity of the (3/2)^n steering word (arXiv:2607.11648), built on the repository's libraries ArithmeticHeights and DiophantineApproximation, whose p-adic Subspace Theorem it uses. Write (3/2)^n = m_n + ε_n with m_n the nearest integer and t_n = 2 m_{n+1} − 3 m_n. The library Stephan2026a is sorry-free and within Lean's three standard axioms. It proves Theorem 1.1, the subword complexity p_T(k) of the steering word T = (t_n) satisfies p_T(k)/k → ∞, together with the numbered results on its proof path: the repetition identity and its corollaries (§2), the reduction to the Diophantine kernel (K) (§3), and the kernel itself, by Ridout-type and three-variable applications of the Subspace Theorem (§4). The open problems of §5 and Conjecture A.2 are stated in Stephan2026a/Problems.lean. Two statements are compared, both forms of Theorem 1.1.

records.name: RPIntro.RPTheoremA
records.entry_name: The regionally proximal relation for commutative semigroup actions
records.doc:
The regionally proximal relation and the equicontinuous structure relation are fundamental relations in topological dynamics that capture equicontinuous behaviour in a topological dynamical system and its factors. For minimal actions of abelian groups they are known to be equivalence relations and to coincide. This development formalizes in Lean 4 the results of the paper "The regionally proximal relation for commutative semigroup actions", which generalizes these facts from group actions to semigroup actions.
Throughout, a system is an action of a discrete semigroup S on a compact Hausdorff space X by continuous maps. A factor is a continuous S-equivariant surjection. The system X is minimal if every orbit is dense, and equicontinuous if the family of maps {s : X -> X} is uniformly equicontinuous. The regionally proximal relation RP consists of the pairs (x,y) such that for all neighbourhoods U of x and V of y and all neighbourhoods a of the diagonal, there are x' in U, y' in V and s in S with (sx', sy') in a. The equicontinuous structure relation Seq consists of the pairs identified by every equicontinuous factor.
The regionally proximal relation has classically been defined only for group actions. The definition used here, for actions of a general semigroup, is the one adopted by Auslander and Dai and by Dai and Xiao; it agrees with the classical notion when the acting semigroup is a group. A second, inequivalent generalization is also natural: the backward regionally proximal relation RP^-, obtained by following the group-action definition of de Vries. For semigroup actions the two differ in general, already for S = (N,+), which is what makes Theorem C below a statement with content.
Theorem A states that for a commutative semigroup S and a minimal S-system X, a factor is equicontinuous exactly when RP is contained in the relation it induces. Theorem B states that RP and Seq coincide; in particular RP is a closed, S-invariant equivalence relation and X -> X/RP is the largest equicontinuous factor of X. Theorem B is apparently new even for systems generated by a single non-invertible map. Theorem C states that RP coincides with the backward regionally proximal relation RP^-, the second natural generalization of regional proximality from groups to semigroups; the two differ in general for semigroup actions, already for S = (N,+). Theorem D states that commuting minimal actions of two commutative semigroups on the same space induce the same regionally proximal relation.
Theorems E and F concern natural extensions. Theorem E constructs, for any minimal action of a commutative semigroup, a smallest extension on which the semigroup acts by homeomorphisms: a minimal S-system W and a factor map W -> X through which every extension of X by homeomorphisms factors. The construction goes through the Grothendieck group Gr(S) of S and requires no cancellativity assumption. Theorem F identifies the largest equicontinuous factor of X with that of its natural extension W, both as an S-system and as a Gr(S)-system.
The proof of Theorem B follows the cube-space methods of Glasner, Gutman and Ye, generalized in places and specialized in others, using ultrafilters in place of enveloping semigroups and nets to simplify formalization. The development runs to roughly 20,000 lines of Lean across 17 files and formalizes every lemma, proposition, corollary and theorem of the paper; the registered statements are Theorems A through F. The same repository also formalizes a companion paper on the local structure of Delta* sets, registered separately as Palomar entry PALOMAR-2026-10-18-000015.

records.name: PottsDiscontinuity.potts_theorem_1_1
records.entry_name: Discontinuity of the phase transition for the planar random-cluster and Potts models with q > 4 (Theorems 1.1 and 1.2)
records.doc: A complete Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 of Duminil-Copin, Gagnebin, Harel, Manolescu and Tassion (arXiv:1611.09877v2). For the q-state Potts model on the square lattice with q > 4, at beta_c = log(1 + sqrt q), the q + 1 box-limit Gibbs measures are distinct and ergodic, each monochromatic measure gives its own colour probability greater than 1/q at the origin, and the inverse correlation length in the diagonal direction is lambda + 2 sum_{k >= 1} (-1)^k tanh(k lambda) / k, where cosh lambda = sqrt(q) / 2, a positive number. For the random-cluster model on the square lattice with q > 4 at p_c = sqrt(q) / (1 + sqrt q), the free and wired box-limit measures differ, the wired measure has an infinite cluster almost surely, the free two-point function between 0 and the diagonal site x_n decays at the same exact rate, and that rate equals sum_{k >= 0} 4 / ((2k + 1) sinh(pi^2 (2k + 1) / (2 lambda))), which is equivalent to 8 exp(-pi^2 / sqrt(q - 4)) as q decreases to 4. The external results the paper cites and the proof uses (Edwards-Sokal coupling, FKG and comparison inequalities, finite energy, ergodicity and the 0-1 law for infinite clusters, planar self-duality, the coordinate Bethe ansatz of the companion paper arXiv:1611.09909, Perron-Frobenius, the analytic implicit function theorem) are proved or taken from Mathlib; uniqueness of the infinite cluster is not needed, and Brouwer's fixed-point theorem comes from a vendored library. The only axioms are propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

For the random-cluster model on the square lattice with q > 4 at p_c = sqrt(q) / (1 + sqrt q), the free and wired box-limit measures differ, the wired measure has an infinite cluster almost surely, the free two-point function between 0 and the diagonal site x_n decays at the same exact rate, and that rate equals sum_{k >= 0} 4 / ((2k + 1) sinh(pi^2 (2k + 1) / (2 lambda))), which is equivalent to 8 exp(-pi^2 / sqrt(q - 4)) as q decreases to 4. The external results the paper cites and the proof uses (Edwards-Sokal coupling, FKG and comparison inequalities, finite energy, ergodicity and the 0-1 law for infinite clusters, planar self-duality, the coordinate Bethe ansatz of the companion paper arXiv:1611.09909, Perron-Frobenius, the analytic implicit function theorem) are proved or taken from Mathlib; uniqueness of the infinite cluster is not needed, and Brouwer's fixed-point theorem comes from a vendored library. The only axioms are propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

records.name: GoldbachLean.Wu2008.WuReal.wu_admissible
records.entry_name: Wu 2008 Lemma 2.2, Chen's double sieve inequality, with the range of the last sum repaired
records.doc: A Lean 4 proof of the combinatorial inequality (2.2) of J. Wu, Chen's double sieve, Goldbach's conjecture and the twin prime problem, 2, Acta Arith. 131 (2008), Lemma 2.2: 4 D_{1,2} >= 3 Y1 + Y2 - Y3 - Y4 + Y5 + Y6 - 2 Y7 - Y8 - Y9 - Y10 - Y11 - error, where the Y_i are Wu's sieve sums over the sequence A = {N - p}. The printed proof drops part of the range of the triple sum produced by Buchstab's identity, so the printed Y11, over p4 < N^{1/2-2 kappa1}/p3, is not justified; this formalization proves the inequality with the full range N^{kappa2} <= p4 < N^{1/2-3 kappa1}, for every N > 1, every pair kappa1, kappa2 meeting Wu's hypotheses, any finite A of integers 0 < a < N coprime to N, and with Wu's O(N^{1-kappa1}) made explicit as 4N/(N^{kappa1}-1) for A = {N - p}. Version 2 adds Lemma 3.1 of R. Li, On Chen's theorem, Goldbach's conjecture and almost prime twins II, which is the same inequality at kappa1 = 1/11.49, kappa2 = 1/6.18 with the same gap, repaired. Lean code written by an AI agent; the statement was checked against the paper by AI reviewers and is offered for human audit.

records.name: ShannonCapacity.indepNum_le
records.entry_name: Lovász's bound on the Shannon capacity
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of Lovász's orthonormal-representation bound on the independence number (if u is an orthonormal representation of G with handle c and 1 ≤ t (c·u_i)² for every vertex, then α(G) ≤ t), of its multiplicativity under strong powers (α(G^⊠k) ≤ t^k), and of its application to the pentagon: α(C₅^⊠k)² ≤ 5^k for every k, Shannon's α(C₅^⊠2) = 5, and hence the Shannon capacity Θ(C₅) = √5. Mathlib has independence numbers but neither strong graph products nor the Shannon capacity.
